title: Tick Tock
summary: Root runs a cleanup script every minute – and anyone can edit it. Make root do something for you.
briefing:
Chapter 3 begins. On the file server dottech-files, root keeps a secret in `/root/flag.txt`. You can't read it – yet.

In chapter 2 you learned that cron runs jobs on a schedule, often as root. This time one of those jobs runs a script that **everyone** may change. Whatever is in that script, root will run it – every single minute.

You now have a new tool: `>` and `>>` write a command's output into a file. `echo hello > note.txt` replaces what is in the file; `echo hello >> note.txt` adds a line at the end.

In DotOS, the clock moves on a minute every time you run a command – `date` shows the time, and `sleep 60` lets a minute pass. You have **written permission** to prove the hole is real.
objective: Add a line to root's cleanup script that copies the flag somewhere you can read it.
debrief:
Root did your job for you! The script `/opt/maintenance/cleanup.sh` had the permissions `-rwxrwxrwx`: anyone could write to it. You added one line with `>>` – for example `cat /root/flag.txt > /tmp/flag.txt` – and a minute later cron ran the script as root, line and all.

This is one of the classic ways attackers become root on Linux: find a script that root runs automatically (in `/etc/crontab`, in systemd timers, in startup scripts) and check who may change it. Your line could just as well have given you a root shell.

The lessons for DotTech: scripts that run as root must be owned by root and writable **only** by root (`chmod 755`, or `700`). "Everyone should be able to tweak it" is not a permission – it is an open door.
hints: Cron runs a script as root every minute, and that script can be changed by anyone. Anything you add to it will run as root the next time.

`cat /etc/crontab` shows the job, `ls -l` shows that its script is writable by everyone. Add a line with `echo '<command>' >> <script>` – a command that copies root's flag into `/tmp`. Then let a minute pass with `sleep 60`.

lines: # Each line: minute hour day month weekday  user  command
# Tidies up the shared folders every minute.
# Everyone in IT should be able to tweak this, so: chmod 777  – Jonas
No sudo, no passwords, no set-user-ID surprises.
But something writes to /var/log/cleanup.log every minute... who?
